--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Machine Guarding and Functional Safety ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - Apply the Hierarchy of Controls to manufacturing safety design - Identify and specify appropriate physical guarding and interlock systems - Select and position presence-sensing devices (light curtains, area scanners) - Calculate safety distances for protective device placement - Understand collaborative robot safety requirements - Design emergency stop systems according to standards - Differentiate between safety integrity levels (SIL) and performance levels (PL) > "Safety isn't expensive, it's priceless." > — Anonymous ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Introduction: The Safety Hierarchy In process engineering, safety is not merely a feature added at the end of a project; it is a **fundamental design constraint**. Before deploying safety devices, the engineer must apply the **Hierarchy of Controls** — a systematic approach to eliminating or reducing workplace hazards. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{5em}llll} \caption{\label{tab:hierarchy-table}Hierarchy of Controls: Detailed Breakdown}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{27AE60}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Priority}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{27AE60}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Control Level}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{27AE60}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Description}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{27AE60}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Example}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{27AE60}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Effectiveness}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{1}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{**Elimination**} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Physically remove the hazard entirely} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Eliminate pinch point by redesigning mechanism} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Most Effective}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{2}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{**Substitution**} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Replace with something less hazardous} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Use lower voltage (24V DC instead of 120V AC)} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Very Effective}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{D6EAF8}{3}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D6EAF8}{**Engineering Controls**} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D6EAF8}{Isolate people from the hazard through design} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D6EAF8}{Install machine guarding, light curtains, interlocks} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D6EAF8}{Effective}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{4}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{**Administrative Controls**} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{Change the way people work} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{Safety procedures, training, warning signs, lock-out/tag-out} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{Less Effective}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{5}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{**PPE**} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Protect the worker with equipment} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Safety glasses, gloves, steel-toe boots, hearing protection} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Least Effective}\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: :::
Discussion: Why not just rely on PPE? **PPE (Personal Protective Equipment)** is the least effective control because: 1. **It doesn't eliminate the hazard** — the danger still exists 2. **It depends on human compliance** — workers may forget or choose not to wear it 3. **It can fail** — equipment degrades, doesn't fit properly, or is damaged 4. **It's the last line of defense** — if PPE fails, the worker is exposed **Key Principle:** The more we can design out hazards through engineering controls, the less we depend on human behavior to keep people safe. > "If you have to post a warning sign, you've already failed at design."
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Physical Guarding and Interlocks Physical barriers are the most intuitive form of protection. They create a "hard" separation between the operator and moving parts, ensuring that humans cannot enter the danger zone during machine operation. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Types of Physical Guarding](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/guarding-types-viz-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Fixed Guards **Fixed guards** are permanent barriers that require tools to remove. They are the simplest and most reliable form of protection. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{12em}l} \caption{\label{tab:fixed-guard-table}Fixed Guards: Key Characteristics}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{3498DB}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Characteristic}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{3498DB}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Description}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Construction} & Wire mesh, polycarbonate sheets, or solid metal panels\\ \textbf{Removal} & Requires tools (screws, bolts) to remove\\ \textbf{Best Application} & Areas that need infrequent access for maintenance only\\ \textbf{Advantages} & Simple, reliable, low cost, no moving parts to fail\\ \textbf{Disadvantages} & Impedes visibility, slows maintenance, can be removed and not replaced\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Interlocked Guards **Interlocked guards** are access points equipped with sensors. When the guard is opened, the safety controller initiates a stop. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Interlocked Guard Operation Principle](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/interlock-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Stop Categories When an interlock is triggered, the machine must stop. The **stop category** determines how this happens: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{8em}llll} \caption{\label{tab:stop-categories}Machine Stop Categories (IEC 60204-1)}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Category}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Type}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Method}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Application}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Example}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{**Category 0**} & Uncontrolled Stop & Immediate removal of power to actuators & Emergency stops, dangerous machines & Press brake E-stop\\ \textbf{**Category 1**} & Controlled Stop & Controlled deceleration, then power removed & High-inertia machines, robots & Industrial robot guard open\\ \textbf{**Category 2**} & Controlled Stop & Controlled stop with power maintained & Process that cannot be interrupted abruptly & CNC spindle during tool change\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Trapped Key Systems (Lock-Out/Tag-Out) **Trapped key systems** use a mechanical sequence to ensure that a machine cannot be energized unless all access keys are returned to the control panel. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Trapped Key System Sequence](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/loto-sequence-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: :::
Case Study: The Fatal Bypass **Incident:** A maintenance worker was killed when a robot arm unexpectedly activated while he was inside a robotic cell. **What Happened:** - The guard interlock had been bypassed with a "defeat device" (a magnet taped to fool the sensor) - Workers had bypassed the interlock because it slowed down troubleshooting - The bypass had been in place for months without management knowledge **Root Causes:** 1. Interlock caused inconvenience during frequent troubleshooting 2. No monitoring system to detect bypasses 3. Culture that tolerated "workarounds" **Lessons Learned:** - Design interlocks that don't impede normal operations - Use tamper-evident or tamper-resistant devices - Regular safety audits to detect bypasses - Zero-tolerance policy for defeating safety devices > **Never bypass a safety device, even temporarily.**
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Presence-Sensing Devices Presence-sensing devices allow for a **"fence-less" environment**, improving visibility and ergonomics while maintaining high safety levels. They detect when a person enters a hazardous zone and trigger a machine stop. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Types of Presence-Sensing Devices](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/presence-sensing-overview-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Light Curtains **Light curtains** use a transmitter and receiver to create an array of infrared beams. If any beam is broken, the safety circuit is interrupted. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Light Curtain Operating Principle](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/light-curtain-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{10em}lll} \caption{\label{tab:light-curtain-specs}Light Curtain Specifications by Application}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{F39C12}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Parameter}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{F39C12}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Finger Detection (14mm)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{F39C12}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Hand Detection (30mm)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{F39C12}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Body Detection (40mm+)}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Resolution} & 14mm beam spacing & 30mm beam spacing & 40mm+ beam spacing\\ \textbf{Height} & 150-1800mm & 300-1800mm & 900-2000mm\\ \textbf{Range} & 0.5-20m & 0.5-20m & 0.5-30m\\ \textbf{Response Time} & 5-15ms & 10-20ms & 15-30ms\\ \textbf{Application} & Point of operation guarding & Perimeter guarding & Area access detection\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Laser Area Scanners **Laser area scanners** use LiDAR technology to monitor a 2D plane. They are highly flexible and allow for programmable zones. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Laser Area Scanner Zones](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/area-scanner-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{12em}ll} \caption{\label{tab:scanner-comparison}Light Curtains vs. Area Scanners}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Feature}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Light Curtains}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Area Scanners}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Detection Type} & Vertical/Linear Barrier & Horizontal/Area Coverage\\ \textbf{Flexibility} & Fixed installation & Programmable zones\\ \textbf{Zone Configuration} & Single detection plane & Multiple warning + safety zones\\ \textbf{Cost} & Generally lower (\$1,000-5,000) & Higher (\$3,000-10,000)\\ \textbf{Best Use Case} & Clear entry/exit points, press brakes & Large open floors, AGV paths, flexible cells\\ \addlinespace \textbf{Environmental Limits} & Dust/debris can cause false trips & More tolerant of dust, outdoor rated available\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Pressure-Sensitive Safety Mats **Pressure-sensitive mats** detect the presence of a person standing on them. They are used primarily in legacy systems or specific zones where optical sensors may be obscured. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Pressure-Sensitive Safety Mat Construction](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/pressure-mat-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: :::
When to Use Pressure Mats vs. Optical Sensors **Use Pressure Mats When:** - Environment has heavy dust, smoke, or steam (blinds optical sensors) - Detection area is well-defined and doesn't change - Workers need to stand in a specific location - Budget is limited **Use Optical Sensors When:** - Flexibility in zone configuration is needed - Environment is relatively clean - Detection area is large or needs to change - Higher integrity level is required **Hybrid Approach:** Many modern systems use both — area scanners for perimeter protection and pressure mats for specific danger zones near the machine.
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Control-Actuated Safety Devices These devices ensure that the operator's body—specifically their hands—is in a predetermined **safe location** before the machine can cycle. ### Two-Hand Controls **Two-hand controls** are common in pressing or stamping operations. To initiate a cycle, the operator must press two buttons simultaneously. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Two-Hand Control System](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/two-hand-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: > **Anti-Tie-Down Requirement:** Modern systems require both buttons to be pressed within **0.5 seconds** of each other. This prevents operators from taping one button down to work with one hand. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{12em}ll} \caption{\label{tab:two-hand-requirements}Two-Hand Control Requirements}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Requirement}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Standard Value}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Purpose}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Synchronous activation} & Within 0.5 seconds & Prevents one-hand operation\\ \textbf{Continuous pressure} & Must be held throughout cycle & Ensures hands stay on controls\\ \textbf{Release before restart} & Both must be released before next cycle & Prevents automatic cycling\\ \textbf{Button spacing} & Minimum 260mm (10 inches) apart & Cannot press both with one hand/arm\\ \textbf{Guards around buttons} & Prevent accidental activation & Prevents hip, elbow, or object activation\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Enable/Deadman Switches **Enable switches** (also called deadman switches) are used during **Teach Mode** for robotics. The operator must hold a three-position trigger in the **middle** position. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Three-Position Enable Switch Operation](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/enable-switch-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: :::
Why Three Positions? The three-position design accounts for **two natural human reactions** to danger: 1. **Panic (Release):** When frightened, people often release what they're holding — robot stops. 2. **Startle (Squeeze):** When startled, people often grip tighter — robot stops. Only a deliberate, controlled **middle hold** allows the robot to move. This is fundamental to safe teach pendant operation.
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Collaborative Robotics (Cobots) **Collaborative robots (cobots)** represent a shift from "separation" to "collaboration." They rely on sophisticated internal sensors rather than external cages, allowing humans and robots to work in the same space. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Traditional Robot vs. Collaborative Robot](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/cobot-comparison-guarding-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Collaborative Operation Methods ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 define **four methods** for safe collaborative operation: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{15em}lll} \caption{\label{tab:cobot-methods}Four Methods of Collaborative Robot Operation}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{2ECC71}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Method}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{2ECC71}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{How It Works}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{2ECC71}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Sensors Used}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{2ECC71}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Application}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{**Safety-Rated Monitored Stop**} & Robot stops when human enters workspace, resumes when clear & Area scanners, light curtains & Large robot needing occasional access\\ \textbf{**Hand Guiding**} & Operator physically guides robot through motions & Force/torque sensors in joints & Teaching, positioning\\ \textbf{**Speed and Separation Monitoring**} & Robot slows or stops based on human proximity & Area scanners, radar, cameras & Shared workspace with varying proximity\\ \textbf{**Power and Force Limiting**} & Robot limits force/power to safe levels on contact & Joint torque sensors & Direct contact applications\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Power and Force Limiting (PFL) The most common cobot safety method is **Power and Force Limiting**. The robot detects a change in torque in its joints. If it bumps into a human, it stops before a regulated amount of force is exceeded. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{12em}rrl} \caption{\label{tab:pfl-limits}ISO/TS 15066 Biomechanical Limits (Quasi-static contact)}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Body Region}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Maximum Pressure (N/cm²)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Maximum Force (N)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Risk Level}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Skull/Forehead}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{130} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{130} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Critical}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Face}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{65} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{65} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Critical}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Neck}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{145} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{150} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Critical}\\ \textbf{Back/Shoulders} & 210 & 210 & Moderate\\ \textbf{Chest} & 140 & 140 & Moderate\\ \addlinespace \textbf{Abdomen} & 110 & 110 & Moderate\\ \textbf{Hand/Fingers} & 300 & 140 & Lower\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: :::
Discussion: Are Cobots Always Safe? **Common Misconception:** "Cobots are safe, so we don't need to do a risk assessment." **Reality:** Cobots are *potentially* safe, but a **risk assessment is always required**. **Factors that can make a cobot unsafe:** 1. **End-of-arm tooling** — A soft gripper is different from a sharp blade 2. **Workpiece** — Carrying a heavy or sharp object increases risk 3. **Speed** — Even force-limited robots can cause injury at high speed 4. **Application** — Some tasks bring humans closer to hazards 5. **Environment** — Slippery floors, confined spaces, etc. > **Every collaborative application requires a documented risk assessment per ISO 12100.**

``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Safety Distance Calculation A safety device cannot be placed arbitrarily. It must be far enough away that the machine comes to a **complete halt** before the human can reach the hazard. ### The Safety Distance Formula The minimum safety distance $S$ is calculated as: $$S = (K \times T) + C$$ Where: - **$K$**: The hand/body approach speed (standardized values) - **$T$**: The total stopping time of the system (device response + machine stop time) - **$C$**: The "penetration depth" (how far a hand can reach through before being detected) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Safety Distance Components](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/safety-distance-viz-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Standard Values for K ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{15em}ll} \caption{\label{tab:k-values}Standard Approach Speed Values (ISO 13855)}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{3498DB}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Approach Type}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{3498DB}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{K Value (mm/s)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{3498DB}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{When to Use}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Hand/Arm Approach (fast)} & 2000 & Close approach to point of operation\\ \textbf{Hand/Arm Approach (normal)} & 1600 & General approach to machines\\ \textbf{Walking Approach} & 1600 & Area access detection\\ \textbf{Standing Reach} & 0 (static) & Worker already in position\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Penetration Depth (C) The penetration depth depends on the **resolution** of the sensing device: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{lll} \caption{\label{tab:c-values}Penetration Depth Values Based on Resolution}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Resolution (mm)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{C Value (mm)}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{9B59B6}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Detection Type}}}\\ \midrule ≤14 & 0 & Finger detection\\ >14 to ≤20 & 80 & Finger/Hand\\ >20 to ≤30 & 130 & Hand detection\\ >30 to ≤40 & 240 & Hand/Arm\\ >40 & 850 & Body detection\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Example Calculation Live cell — try different approach speed, response time, or resolution values. ```{webr-r} #| label: safety-calc-example # Given parameters K <- 2000 # Approach speed (mm/s) - fast hand approach T_device <- 0.020 # Light curtain response time (20 ms = 0.020 s) T_machine <- 0.150 # Machine stopping time (150 ms = 0.150 s) C <- 0 # Penetration depth for 14mm resolution # Calculate total stopping time T_total <- T_device + T_machine cat("Total stopping time (T):", T_total * 1000, "ms\n") # Calculate minimum safety distance S <- (K * T_total) + C cat("Minimum safety distance (S):", S, "mm\n") cat("Minimum safety distance (S):", S / 25.4, "inches\n") # Interpretation cat("\n--- Interpretation ---\n") cat("The light curtain must be at least", S, "mm from the hazard.\n") cat("This ensures the machine stops before a person can reach the danger zone.\n") ```
Practice Problem: Calculate Safety Distance **Given:** - Light curtain resolution: 30mm (hand detection) - Light curtain response time: 15ms - Machine stopping time: 200ms - Application: Operator hand approach **Calculate the minimum safety distance.** **Solution:** ``` K = 1600 mm/s (normal hand approach) T = 0.015 + 0.200 = 0.215 seconds C = 130 mm (for 30mm resolution) S = (K × T) + C S = (1600 × 0.215) + 130 S = 344 + 130 S = 474 mm (approximately 18.7 inches) ``` The light curtain must be installed at least **474mm** from the nearest hazard point.
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Emergency Stop (E-Stop) Systems The **Emergency Stop** is the "last resort" — it is not a safety device but a **complementary protective measure**. It must be available to stop the machine when all other measures have failed. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![E-Stop Design Requirements](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/estop-design-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{10em}l} \caption{\label{tab:estop-requirements}E-Stop Requirements per IEC 60204-1}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Requirement}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{E74C3C}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Standard}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{Color} & Red (RAL 3000 or equivalent)\\ \textbf{Shape} & Mushroom head (palm or fist operated)\\ \textbf{Background} & Yellow (high contrast)\\ \textbf{Operation} & Self-latching (stays activated when pressed)\\ \textbf{Reset} & Manual reset required (twist, pull, or key)\\ \addlinespace \textbf{Accessibility} & Within easy reach of all operators\\ \textbf{Wiring} & Normally closed contacts (fail-safe)\\ \textbf{Function} & Category 0 or Category 1 stop\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### E-Stop Pull Cords For long conveyors or machines where an operator cannot quickly reach a fixed button, **pull cords** provide continuous E-Stop coverage. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![E-Stop Pull Cord System](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/pull-cord-diagram-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: :::
Common E-Stop Mistakes **Mistake 1: Using E-Stop for normal stopping** - E-Stops are for emergencies only - Normal stops should use a separate control - Frequent E-Stop use causes wear and desensitizes operators **Mistake 2: E-Stop that doesn't stop everything** - All hazardous motion must stop - Auxiliary equipment (conveyors, feeders) often forgotten - Review entire system, not just the primary machine **Mistake 3: Automatic restart after E-Stop reset** - Machine must NOT automatically restart when E-Stop is released - Separate "Start" action required - This prevents unexpected motion after reset **Mistake 4: Hidden or blocked E-Stops** - E-Stops must be visible and accessible - Guard placement sometimes blocks access - Regular audits needed to ensure accessibility
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Functional Safety Standards Modern safety systems must meet specific **performance levels** to ensure reliability. Two main frameworks exist: ### Safety Integrity Levels (SIL) - IEC 62061 ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{}llll} \caption{\label{tab:sil-levels}Safety Integrity Levels (PFH = Probability of Dangerous Failure per Hour)}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{8E44AD}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{SIL Level}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{8E44AD}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{PFH Range}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{8E44AD}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Approximate Meaning}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{8E44AD}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Typical Application}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{SIL 1}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{≥10⁻⁶ to <10⁻⁵} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Dangerous failure less than once per 11 years} & \cellcolor[HTML]{D5F5E3}{Low-risk tasks}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{SIL 2}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{≥10⁻⁷ to <10⁻⁶} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{Dangerous failure less than once per 114 years} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FEF9E7}{Most industrial machinery}\\ \textbf{\cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{SIL 3}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{≥10⁻⁸ to <10⁻⁷} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{Dangerous failure less than once per 1,140 years} & \cellcolor[HTML]{FADBD8}{High-risk processes}\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ### Performance Levels (PL) - ISO 13849-1 ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{}llll} \caption{\label{tab:pl-levels}Performance Levels per ISO 13849-1}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{16A085}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Performance Level}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{16A085}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{PFH Range}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{16A085}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Risk Reduction}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{16A085}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Equivalent SIL}}}\\ \midrule \textbf{PL a} & ≥10⁻⁵ to <10⁻⁴ & Lowest & < SIL 1\\ \textbf{PL b} & ≥3×10⁻⁶ to <10⁻⁵ & Low & SIL 1\\ \textbf{PL c} & ≥10⁻⁶ to <3×10⁻⁶ & Medium & SIL 1\\ \textbf{PL d} & ≥10⁻⁷ to <10⁻⁶ & High & SIL 2\\ \textbf{PL e} & ≥10⁻⁸ to <10⁻⁷ & Highest & SIL 3\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Relationship Between SIL and PL](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/sil-pl-relationship-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: :::
Which Standard to Use: SIL or PL? **Use ISO 13849-1 (Performance Levels) when:** - Designing safety functions for standard machinery - Using off-the-shelf safety components - Simpler systems with well-defined safety functions **Use IEC 62061 (SIL) when:** - Complex programmable systems (safety PLCs) - Process industries - When customer or regulation specifies SIL **Note:** Many modern systems use both standards, as they are harmonized and can be used together. The choice often depends on industry practice and customer requirements.
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Risk Assessment Process Before selecting any safety device, a **risk assessment** must be performed. This is required by ISO 12100. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Risk Assessment Process (ISO 12100)](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/risk-assessment-process-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Risk Estimation Risk is typically estimated using three factors: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Risk Estimation Matrix](06-Machine-Guarding-and-Safety_files/figure-pdf/risk-matrix-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Summary ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} \begin{longtable}[t]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{15em}ll} \caption{\label{tab:summary-table-ch6}Machine Guarding and Safety: Key Concepts Summary}\\ \toprule \cellcolor[HTML]{2C3E50}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Topic}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{2C3E50}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Key Points}}} & \cellcolor[HTML]{2C3E50}{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Critical Remember}}}\\ \midrule **Hierarchy of Controls** & Elimination > Substitution > Engineering > Administrative > PPE & Always start at the top of the hierarchy\\ **Physical Guarding** & Fixed guards, interlocked gates, trapped key systems & Stop category (0, 1, 2) determines how machine stops\\ **Presence Sensing** & Light curtains, area scanners, pressure mats & Resolution determines detection capability\\ **Control-Actuated Devices** & Two-hand controls, enable/deadman switches & Anti-tie-down prevents one-hand bypass\\ **Collaborative Robots** & PFL, speed/separation monitoring, hand guiding & Risk assessment required for every cobot application\\ \addlinespace **Safety Distance** & S = (K × T) + C formula for device placement & Include device response AND machine stop time\\ **E-Stop Systems** & Red mushroom on yellow, self-latching, manual reset & E-Stop is last resort, not normal operation\\ **Functional Safety** & SIL (IEC 62061) and PL (ISO 13849-1) standards & Required performance level from risk assessment\\ \bottomrule \end{longtable} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Review Questions
Question 1: What are the five levels of the Hierarchy of Controls, and why is PPE the least effective? The five levels are (from most to least effective): 1. **Elimination** — Physically remove the hazard 2. **Substitution** — Replace with something less hazardous 3. **Engineering Controls** — Isolate people from the hazard 4. **Administrative Controls** — Change how people work 5. **PPE** — Protect the worker with equipment **PPE is least effective because:** - The hazard still exists - It depends on human compliance - Equipment can fail or be worn incorrectly - It's the last line of defense
Question 2: A light curtain has a response time of 12ms and resolution of 14mm. The machine takes 180ms to stop. Calculate the minimum safety distance for hand approach. **Given:** - K = 2000 mm/s (hand approach, use higher value for safety) - T = 0.012 + 0.180 = 0.192 seconds - C = 0 mm (14mm resolution) **Calculation:** $$S = (K \times T) + C$$ $$S = (2000 \times 0.192) + 0$$ $$S = 384 \text{ mm}$$ The light curtain must be installed at least **384mm** (approximately 15 inches) from the hazard.
Question 3: Explain why a three-position enable switch stops the robot in both position 1 (released) and position 3 (fully pressed). The three-position design accounts for two natural human reactions to danger: **Position 1 (Released):** - When frightened, people often release what they're holding (panic response) - Robot stops immediately **Position 3 (Fully Pressed):** - When startled, people often grip tighter (startle response) - Robot stops immediately **Position 2 (Middle):** - Only a deliberate, controlled hold allows operation - Requires conscious effort to maintain - This ensures the operator is alert and in control
Question 4: What are the four methods of collaborative robot operation according to ISO 10218? 1. **Safety-Rated Monitored Stop** - Robot stops when human enters workspace - Resumes when human leaves - Uses area scanners or light curtains 2. **Hand Guiding** - Operator physically guides robot - Force/torque sensors enable safe teaching 3. **Speed and Separation Monitoring** - Robot speed varies based on human proximity - Uses external sensors to track human position 4. **Power and Force Limiting (PFL)** - Robot limits contact force to safe levels - Built-in joint torque sensors - Most common cobot method
Question 5: What are the requirements for an E-Stop button according to IEC 60204-1? **Physical Requirements:** - **Color:** Red - **Shape:** Mushroom head (palm or fist operated) - **Background:** Yellow (high contrast) **Functional Requirements:** - **Self-latching:** Stays activated when pressed - **Manual reset:** Requires deliberate action to release - **Accessibility:** Within easy reach of all operators - **Wiring:** Normally closed contacts (fail-safe) - **Function:** Category 0 or Category 1 stop - **No automatic restart:** Separate start action required after reset
